prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The scene is close-range and downward-facing: the camera wearer’s torso, lap, and arms occupy the nearest foreground, while paving stones, tools, and other people’s lower bodies lie farther below and around them. Across frames 1–3, a person’s jeans and shoes remain roughly 0.7–1.5 m ahead/left, with stones and the tape measure about 0.4–1.0 m in front; in frames 4–5, the camera wearer turns right, bringing a blue vertical object and another person’s legs into the right/front region at roughly 0.7–1.5 m. Brightness makes the wearer’s arms and lap clearly within arm’s reach and separates them from the darker ground and background, while nearby stones and tools are also reachable; substantial self-occlusion hides the central ground. The map reveals coarse near/far layering that is harder to judge from RGB, but absolute metre estimates are uncertain, similarly colored depth regions merge, and thin objects such as the tape, hands, and stone edges have unreliable or blurred boundaries.
descriptions.segmentation: The map identifies several people around the camera wearer, plus a book-like rectangular object near the center in frames 2–3 and cellphone-labeled handheld objects in frames 4–5; the RGB context suggests some of these class labels are incorrect, including labels such as skateboard or book on construction items. The large central person mask is the camera wearer at near-zero to roughly 0.6 m, while partial person masks at the left, center-front, and right correspond to nearby people roughly 0.7–1.5 m away; masks overlap where the wearer’s body or arms block them. From frames 1–3 the closest other person stays mainly ahead/left, then in frames 4–5 the view rotates right and additional partial people and raised arms appear across the front/right; several bodies extend beyond the top or side boundaries, so facing direction and eye contact cannot be established reliably. The masks make instance boundaries, lateral ordering, and occlusion more explicit than RGB alone, but they provide no direct metric depth, fragment single people into pieces, miss most stones and tools, and attach unreliable class labels to small objects.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only hands: a hand lies left/front in frame 1, another appears near the upper-center in frame 2, frame 3 has no stable detection, frame 4 shows a hand/forearm configuration near the lower center-left, and frame 5 shows a raised hand near the upper-right. These detections locate hands relative to the camera and indicate changes caused by camera turning or limb movement, with the frame-4 hand roughly within 0.3–0.8 m and the other detected hands approximately 0.7–1.5 m away, although the map itself does not encode metric distance. The isolated hand skeletons help separate finger and wrist geometry from the cluttered RGB and show that the frame-5 hand is above and right of the camera wearer, while the frame-1 hand is lower and left. No usable body skeletons are present, so full posture, facing direction, gaze, person-to-person spacing, and reach cannot be inferred reliably; detections are intermittent, partly clipped, and may omit or misconnect occluded fingers.
